name: Suparshvanatha
role: Seventh Tirthankara of the present age
summary: In Jain tradition Suparshvanatha is the seventh of the 24 Tirthankaras of this descending age, born in Varanasi, shown with a golden glow and a gentle five-headed serpent hood.
about: Jain texts count Suparshvanatha as the seventh Tirthankara, a teacher who shows the path across the cycle of rebirth. He is said to have been born in Varanasi to King Pratishtha and Queen Prithvi of the Ikshvaku family. Digambara texts say his mother saw sixteen auspicious dreams before his birth, while Shvetambaras count fourteen for a Tirthankara's mother. As a prince he looked after his people, but according to the tradition, falling leaves and wilting flowers made him think about how everything fades. He handed the kingdom to his son and became an ascetic. After about nine months he is said to have reached omniscience (kevala jnana). Jains believe he attained liberation on Mount Shikharji in present-day Jharkhand. Sources differ on small details such as his colour, which is golden in some texts and green in others.
kidSummary: Suparshvanatha is the seventh Tirthankara, a wise teacher in Jainism. Jain stories say he was a prince in Varanasi who cared for his people. One day, they say, seeing leaves fall and flowers droop, he understood that nothing lasts forever, and he chose a life of quiet meditation.

story.title: A prince of Varanasi
story.text: Long ago, Jains say, a prince named Suparshvanatha was born in the city of Varanasi. His mother is said to have seen a series of lovely dreams before he arrived.

story.title: A caring king
story.text: Jain stories say that when he grew up he became king after his father. He looked after his people and made sure the kingdom ran well.

story.title: Leaves and flowers
story.text: Tradition says he noticed leaves falling and flowers wilting one day. He realised that all things in the world change and fade.

story.title: Choosing the quiet path
story.text: He gave the kingdom to his son and became a wandering monk. After months of meditation, Jains say, he gained perfect knowledge.

story.title: Sharing what he knew
story.text: He then taught others how to live without harming anyone. At the end of his life he reached liberation on Mount Shikharji.

teaches: Everything in the world changes, so do not cling
Care for others, even when you lead

facts.text: His name is often explained as good sides (su = good, parshva = side). One tale says his mother had leprosy on both sides of her body, but it was cured before he was born.
The Buddhist Mahavagga mentions a shrine of Suparshvanatha at Rajgir in the Buddha's own time, one of the early outside hints that Jain worship was already established.

Images of him show a hood of five serpent heads over his head with no coils behind, while Parshvanatha is shown with seven or more heads and coils. Beneath his feet, Shvetambara images carry the swastika, an ancient sign of well-being, as his marker.
A verse about him in the Svayambhustotra compares the body to a vehicle that needs a driver and calls the soul its operator, so it is pointless to cling to the body.
One medieval iconography manual, the Aparajitaprccha, makes him green, while many images show him golden, so sources disagree on his colour.

At Mathura an old stupa carries a 157 CE inscription saying an image of the Tirthankara Aranatha was set up at a stupa built by the gods. Two medieval writers, Somadeva Suri and Jinaprabha Suri, say the stupa was raised for Suparshvanatha.
The Supasnath Chariyam, a manuscript about his life, was compiled in 1422-23 at Dilwara during the reign of Mokkhal.
Jain texts give his height as 200 bows and his lifespan as 20 lakh purvas, and say he lived as a prince, then a married king, before renouncing.
Inside the 15th-century Ranakpur Jain temple complex in Rajasthan, one temple has him as its main deity.
The Yajurveda is said to contain a word spelled like his name, but it is an epithet meaning All-Pure Lord and has a different sense.

quiz.q: Which city is Suparshvanatha said to be born in?
quiz.why: Jain texts place his birth in Varanasi, where a temple in Bhadaini marks it.

quiz.q: What made him think about leaving his kingdom?
quiz.why: Seeing leaves fall and flowers fade reminded him that all things change.

quiz.q: On his images, which snake feature shields his head?
quiz.why: Parshvanatha is the one shown with seven or more heads.

quiz.q: Which mountain is where he is said to have reached liberation?
quiz.why: Shikharji in Jharkhand is the great Jain site of liberation.
